segments: Core Architecture: What Is a UKI?

A UKI (Unified Kernel Image) combines a UEFI boot stub, Linux kernel, initial RAM filesystem, and optional resources into a single .efi executable. It can include microcode, a command line, system identification, and a splash screen.
Reasons to Choose a UKI

Signature coverage of components: a signed UKI verified by Secure Boot can protect its kernel and initramfs. The protection still depends on trusted certificates, firmware policy, and the boot chain; it does not guarantee that arbitrary configuration files cannot be exploited.
Version coupling: keeping the kernel and initramfs together reduces mismatches between separate files; generation and upgrade failures still require a recovery entry point.
Automatic discovery: systemd-boot can discover conforming UKIs under /EFI/Linux/ on the ESP or XBOOTLDR partition.
UKI Generation Workflow
Choosing Tools
mkinitcpio can generate UKIs; with systemd-ukify installed, ukify can assemble them. Choose one generation pipeline to avoid multiple tools overwriting each other's output.

Installation writes to the ESP and may create firmware boot entries. For automatic updates, also check whether systemd-boot-update.service is actually enabled and verify the signing workflow. Running bootctl install alone does not complete all maintenance configuration.
Secure Boot Signing Workflow
Key Creation, Enrollment, and Saving Signing Paths

Read the device's firmware documentation first, back up the existing keys, and preserve recovery options. The firmware must allow entering Setup Mode. Replacing keys incorrectly may prevent some devices' Option ROMs, displays, or other operating systems from starting.

-m adds Microsoft certificates, a trade-off between compatibility and the scope of trust. sign -s saves file paths for subsequent signing workflows. Automatic re-signing after updates also depends on sbctl's mkinitcpio, kernel-install, or pacman hooks actually taking effect.
TPM2 Measurements and Disk Unlocking
systemd-stub measures UKI components into PCR 11. Static PCR binding ties key unsealing to selected measurement values; it is not a blanket proof that “the system has never been tampered with.”

Direct binding to PCR 11 may stop working after a UKI update, and measurement values continue changing during boot phases. Design a signed PCR policy or another supported strategy for the actual systemd version, and test updates, firmware changes, and recovery paths. TPM-based automatic unlocking also does not replace access controls on the running system.
